Provable Coordination for LLM Agents via Message Sequence Charts

Benedikt Bollig Affiliation: Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, ENS Paris-Saclay, LMF, Gif-sur-Yvette, France    Matthias Függer Affiliation: Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, ENS Paris-Saclay, LMF, Gif-sur-Yvette, France    Thomas Nowak Affiliation: Université Paris-Saclay, CNRS, ENS Paris-Saclay, LMF, Gif-sur-Yvette, France Affiliation: Institut Universitaire de France, Paris, France
Abstract

Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are difficult to reason about. Coordination errors such as deadlocks or type-mismatched messages are often hard to detect through testing. We introduce a domain-specific language for specifying agent coordination based on message sequence charts (MSCs). The language separates message-passing structure from LLM actions, whose outputs remain unpredictable. We define the syntax and semantics of the language and present a syntax-directed projection that generates deadlock-free local agent programs from global coordination specifications. We illustrate the approach with a diagnosis consensus protocol and show how coordination properties can be established independently of LLM nondeterminism. We also describe a runtime planning extension in which an LLM dynamically generates a coordination workflow for which the same structural guarantees apply. An open-source Python implementation of our framework is available as ZipperGen.

Keywords: 
Agent coordination Message Sequence Charts Formal semantics Large language models

1 Introduction

Multi-agent systems built on large language models (LLMs) are increasingly common. They combine the capabilities of individual AI components with the structural advantages of distributed systems, such as concurrency, separation of concerns, and explicit communication patterns. A typical example is a group of LLM agents that iteratively exchange assessments until they reach agreement on a task, such as giving a medical diagnosis.

These systems are, however, hard to design and to reason about. While classical distributed systems are already notoriously error prone, the stochastic nature of LLM outputs further complicates reasoning about such systems. When agents exchange messages and collaborate, problems such as deadlocks or lost messages are difficult to rule out through testing alone. Frameworks like LangGraph [17], AutoGen [25], and CrewAI [5] provide convenient infrastructure for building such systems, but offer no formal guarantees. The broader engineering challenges of such systems, such as transparency, traceability, and error attribution, are well-documented [7]. Applying formal methods to this setting is therefore natural.

Contributions.

For this purpose, we propose a domain-specific language (DSL) for agent coordination based on message sequence charts (MSCs) [16], an International Telecommunication Union (ITU) standard for communication protocols. MSCs combine a visual notation with a formal semantics. They represent both the local progress of individual agents (their lifelines) and the messages exchanged between them, making causal dependencies in a system execution easy to track.

Abstractly, an MSC describes a single execution. Higher-level formalisms compose simple MSCs into sets (or languages). They can be thought of as global workflows: specifications of what a distributed system should do, independently of how it is implemented. Much research has addressed the question of how such global specifications can be realized in a distributed fashion. The conceptually cleanest approach is projection: deriving a local program for each participant by restricting the global specification to that participant’s view. This has been pursued both for MSC-based formalisms [1, 10, 3] and for multiparty session types (MPST) [15, 18]. These works follow an automata-theoretic route: a realizability condition is checked, local machines are constructed, and correctness is established by language equivalence.

Our approach works with structured programs rather than automata and targets LLM components directly. Workflow-level specifications suit LLM agents well: rather than following a finite transition graph, agents maintain variable-length context, evaluate local conditions, and branch based on their own state. Moreover, the projected local programs are programs again: they can be embedded in larger workflows, exposed as APIs, or composed with other components without further translation. Existing LLM-based multi-agent frameworks do not address the synthesis of provably correct distributed agent programs.

The same holds when the coordination structure is not fixed in advance but generated at runtime by a planning LLM. Asking such a system to produce deadlock-free distributed code directly is unreasonable: it would have to ensure that every send by one agent is matched by a receive of another, in every branch and under every execution order. With our language, the planner needs only to produce a syntactically valid global workflow. Deadlock-freedom is then guaranteed by the projection. The language is therefore not only a programming interface for humans, but also a natural target for LLM-based planning.

We extend standard MSCs with two constructs: action blocks, which treat LLM computations as opaque typed functions, and owned control flow, where each conditional and loop has an explicit decider. The first extension separates what can be guaranteed statically (the message-passing structure, which has a precise operational semantics) from what cannot: the stochastic outputs of LLM calls. The second makes projection syntax-directed: it is a structural recursion on the global workflow, and the correctness proof is a structural induction. No automaton is constructed at any point.

Related work.

Our work connects two lines of research. The first is the formal side: realizability for MSCs and communicating automata [1, 9, 10, 3, 21, 20, 19, 24, 11] addresses the question of whether a global specification admits a deadlock-free distributed implementation. Rather than solving this problem post-hoc, we follow a by-construction approach: the global language is designed so that projection is always syntax-directed and yields well-structured local programs directly. Closest to our approach is [9], which also inserts control messages automatically to synthesize local controllers, but works with automaton-based global specifications and is not designed for LLM-based agents.

Multiparty session types (MPSTs) [14, 15, 18, 6, 4, 8] also project a global description to local views, but require well-formedness conditions for projection to be defined, notably that uninvolved participants have consistent local behaviors across branches. Scribble [26] is a prominent practical MPST-based protocol language, and its refinement-typed extension [27] further adds data-level verification, an orthogonal direction we do not pursue. In contrast, our language is designed so that projection is always defined for its constructs: owned control flow together with explicit control broadcasts eliminates the need for such consistency conditions (often formulated as branch-mergeability [8]) in standard MPST settings. Process calculi [13, 22] work in the opposite direction: local processes are composed to obtain global behavior, rather than projected from a global specification.

The second line concerns practical multi-agent frameworks such as LangGraph, AutoGen, and CrewAI [17, 25, 5]. These treat coordination as an engineering concern, relying on testing and runtime monitoring for correctness. We separate the coordination layer from the LLM layer and reason about the former independently; in particular, deadlock-freedom holds even for runtime-generated workflows, which to our knowledge no existing framework guarantees.

Outline.

Section 2 presents introductory examples. Sections 3–4 define the syntax and semantics of global and local programs. Section 5 presents the projection, proves correctness and deadlock-freedom, and describes the ZipperGen implementation (https://zippergen.io). Section 6 illustrates the framework. Section 7 concludes. Proofs are deferred to the appendix.

2 Introductory Examples

We illustrate our language on a simple multi-agent workflow.

The program in Listing 1 specifies a review-before-action workflow with four lifelines: 𝑃𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑛𝑒𝑟\mathit{Planner}, 𝑅𝑒𝑣𝑖𝑒𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{Reviewer}, 𝐸𝑥𝑒𝑐𝑢𝑡𝑜𝑟\mathit{Executor}, and 𝑂𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑜𝑟\mathit{Orchestrator}. Planner receives a task, produces a plan, and decides whether it needs review. In the first scenario (𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑛​_​𝑛𝑒𝑒𝑑𝑠​_​𝑟𝑒𝑣𝑖𝑒𝑤\mathit{plan\_needs\_review} is true), Planner sends the plan to Reviewer, who critiques it and forwards the critique to Orchestrator. In the second scenario, the review is skipped. In both cases, Planner forwards the plan to Executor, whose result is sent to Orchestrator, which finalizes the outcome.

Figure 1 gives a graphical view of the workflow, abstracting away variable declarations and types. The dashed box separates the two branches of the conditional; the figure thus represents two MSCs, one per scenario. Action blocks such as 𝚊𝚌𝚝​𝑃𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑛𝑒𝑟:(𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑛,𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑛​_​𝑛𝑒𝑒𝑑𝑠​_​𝑟𝑒𝑣𝑖𝑒𝑤)=𝑚𝑎𝑘𝑒​_​𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑛​(𝑡𝑎𝑠𝑘)\mathtt{act}\ \mathit{Planner}:(\mathit{plan},\mathit{plan\_needs\_review})=\mathit{make\_plan}(\mathit{task}) model opaque AI computations. The conditional 𝚒𝚏​𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑛​_​𝑛𝑒𝑒𝑑𝑠​_​𝑟𝑒𝑣𝑖𝑒𝑤​@​𝑃𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑛𝑒𝑟\mathtt{if}\ \mathit{plan\_needs\_review}@\mathit{Planner} has an owned decider: only 𝑃𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑛𝑒𝑟\mathit{Planner} chooses the branch, and 𝑅𝑒𝑣𝑖𝑒𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{Reviewer} participates only in the true branch. The last action depends on both 𝑐𝑟𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑞𝑢𝑒\mathit{critique} and 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑢𝑙𝑡\mathit{result}. Thus, computations remain opaque, but the coordination around them is made explicit. The return statement designates the output lifeline; it is not part of the MSC but specifies which lifeline’s value is returned to the caller. Note that the critique is sent to 𝑂𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑜𝑟\mathit{Orchestrator} rather than back to 𝑃𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑛𝑒𝑟\mathit{Planner}: the review influences the final outcome but does not block execution.

The program above is written from a global viewpoint: it describes the full coordination of all lifelines in a single text. In practice, each agent runs its own local program and communicates with the others exclusively by sending and receiving messages over first-in first-out (FIFO) channels. FIFO channels allow agents to overlap their work. A sender can deposit a message and continue immediately, and the receiver picks it up whenever its local execution reaches the corresponding receive. This allows agents that do not depend on each other to proceed in parallel.

One obvious implementation strategy is simple polling: each agent repeatedly checks its incoming channels and processes the first available message. But this is not sufficient even for programs satisfying the local property of [10] or the local-choice property of [2, 12]. Consider the true branch of reviewed_execution. Once 𝑃𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑛𝑒𝑟\mathit{Planner} has sent the plan to 𝑅𝑒𝑣𝑖𝑒𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{Reviewer}, its participation in the if-block is complete, and it immediately sends the plan to 𝐸𝑥𝑒𝑐𝑢𝑡𝑜𝑟\mathit{Executor}. As a result, 𝑅𝑒𝑣𝑖𝑒𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{Reviewer} and 𝐸𝑥𝑒𝑐𝑢𝑡𝑜𝑟\mathit{Executor} run concurrently and both send their outputs to 𝑂𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑜𝑟\mathit{Orchestrator}. Because the channels are asynchronous, 𝐸𝑥𝑒𝑐𝑢𝑡𝑜𝑟\mathit{Executor} may finish and deliver 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑢𝑙𝑡\mathit{result} to 𝑂𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑜𝑟\mathit{Orchestrator} before 𝑅𝑒𝑣𝑖𝑒𝑤𝑒𝑟\mathit{Reviewer} has even dequeued the plan. This prefix execution is reachable under polling, yet it cannot be extended to a valid completion: 𝑂𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑜𝑟\mathit{Orchestrator} dequeues 𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑢𝑙𝑡\mathit{result} before 𝑐𝑟𝑖𝑡𝑖𝑞𝑢𝑒\mathit{critique} arrives. Our projection overcomes this by having 𝑃𝑙𝑎𝑛𝑛𝑒𝑟\mathit{Planner} broadcast an explicit control message that tells 𝑂𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑜𝑟\mathit{Orchestrator} which branch was taken. 𝑂𝑟𝑐ℎ𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑜𝑟\mathit{Orchestrator}’s local program then enforces the correct receive order (cf. Section 5).

In fact, such control messages are necessary in general. Consider the program below, where AA repeatedly tosses a coin and BB performs a local step in each iteration:

𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎ℎ𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑠@A𝚍𝚘{𝚊𝚌𝚝A:ℎ𝑒𝑎𝑑𝑠=𝑡𝑜𝑠𝑠();𝚊𝚌𝚝B:b=𝑠𝑡𝑒𝑝()}𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝{ε}\mathtt{while}\ \mathit{heads}\texttt{@}A\ \mathtt{do}\ \{\,\mathtt{act}\ A:\mathit{heads}=\mathit{toss}()\ ;\ \mathtt{act}\ B:\mathit{b}=\mathit{step}()\\ \,\}\ \mathtt{exit}\ \{\,\varepsilon\,\}

AA and BB must execute the same number of iterations, yet the iteration count is determined solely by AA’s coin tosses, which are private to AA. There is no user message that BB could observe to recover it. Any correct distributed implementation must therefore send BB an explicit control signal at each iteration, exactly as our projection does.

Most work on MSC realizability, e.g., [1, 21, 19, 10, 20, 24], formulates the question as a decision problem (given a global specification, does a deadlock-free distributed implementation exist?) or identifies sufficient syntactic criteria for it. In practice, one wants simply to write a program and have it run. The constraint is even less realistic when workflows are generated at runtime by a planning LLM, which cannot be expected to produce only specifications satisfying a non-trivial syntactic condition. Our language is designed with this in mind.

3 Global Workflows

A global workflow describes the full coordination structure of a multi-agent system in a single, centralized specification. Rather than programming each agent separately, the developer writes one workflow that captures which agents communicate, in what order, and who owns each control decision. This section defines the formal syntax and semantics of such global workflows.

3.1 Syntax

Throughout this section, fix a finite set ℒ\mathscr{L} of lifelines and a set ℱ\mathscr{F} of action symbols. We use A,B∈ℒA,B\in\mathscr{L} for lifelines, f∈ℱf\in\mathscr{F} for local computations such as LLM calls or deterministic helper functions, x→,y→\vec{x},\vec{y} for payload tuples, and cc for Boolean conditions involving Boolean variables of designated lifelines. Communication proceeds over directed unbounded FIFO channels: for every ordered pair (A,B)(A,B) of distinct lifelines there is one channel A→BA\to B.

Definition 1 (Abstract syntax)

The set 𝖶𝗈𝗋𝗄\mathsf{Work} of global workflows is generated by the following grammar:

P::=\displaystyle P~::=~ ε∣𝚖𝚜𝚐A(x→)→B(y→)∣𝚊𝚌𝚝A:y→=f(x→)∣P1;P2∣\displaystyle\varepsilon~\mid~\mathtt{msg}\ A(\vec{x})\to B(\vec{y})~\mid~\mathtt{act}\ A:\vec{y}=f(\vec{x})~\mid~P_{1};P_{2}~\mid~
𝚒𝚏​c​@​B​𝚝𝚑𝚎𝚗​P⊤​𝚎𝚕𝚜𝚎​P⊥|𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎​c​@​B​𝚍𝚘​P𝑏𝑜𝑑𝑦​𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝​P𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡\displaystyle\mathtt{if}\ c@B\ \mathtt{then}\ P_{\top}\ \mathtt{else}\ P_{\bot}~\mid~\mathtt{while}\ c@B\ \mathtt{do}\ P_{\mathit{body}}\ \mathtt{exit}\ P_{\mathit{exit}}

For message statements, we require distinct endpoints: in 𝚖𝚜𝚐​A​(x→)→B⁡(y→)\mathtt{msg}\ A(\vec{x})\to B(\vec{y}) we assume A≠BA\neq B (no self channels). Payload components in x→=(x1,…,xm)\vec{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}) and y→=(y1,…,yn)\vec{y}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{n}) may be variables or concrete values, such as the truth values ⊤\top (true) and ⊥\bot (false). In action statements 𝚊𝚌𝚝​A:y→=f⁡(x→)\mathtt{act}\ A:\vec{y}=f(\vec{x}), the outputs y→\vec{y} must be variables (assignment targets), while the inputs x→\vec{x} may be variables or constants. Each lifeline maintains its own local variable store. Variable names are scoped per lifeline, so distinct lifelines may use the same name independently.

We emphasize that the grammar contains no return statement. A return is not a coordination step: it does not send a message, perform a computation, or affect any other lifeline. It names the lifeline that produces the final value and the variable holding it. We therefore treat it as a declaration outside the formal language and it plays no role in the projection or the correctness proofs. In the ZipperGen implementation, return var @ AA serves as this declaration and is checked syntactically.

The statements have the following intuitive meaning (Listing 1 illustrates all of them except the while construct):

  • •

    𝚖𝚜𝚐​A​(x→)→B⁡(y→)\mathtt{msg}\ A(\vec{x})\to B(\vec{y}): a communication step in which AA sends a payload tuple and BB receives it, possibly binding components to local variables.

  • •

    𝚊𝚌𝚝​A:y→=f⁡(x→)\mathtt{act}\ A:\vec{y}=f(\vec{x}): a local computation performed by lifeline AA; in Listing 1, examples are 𝑚𝑎𝑘𝑒​_​𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑛\mathit{make\_plan}, 𝑟𝑒𝑣𝑖𝑒𝑤​_​𝑝𝑙𝑎𝑛\mathit{review\_plan}, and 𝑓𝑖𝑛𝑎𝑙𝑖𝑧𝑒\mathit{finalize}.

  • •

    𝚒𝚏​c​@​B​𝚝𝚑𝚎𝚗​P⊤​𝚎𝚕𝚜𝚎​P⊥\mathtt{if}\ c@B\ \mathtt{then}\ P_{\top}\ \mathtt{else}\ P_{\bot}: a conditional whose branch is chosen exclusively by lifeline BB. The annotation @​B@B records this ownership explicitly, even though the branch programs P⊤P_{\top} and P⊥P_{\bot} may themselves involve several lifelines.

  • •

    𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎​c​@​B​𝚍𝚘​P𝑏𝑜𝑑𝑦​𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝​P𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡\mathtt{while}\ c@B\ \mathtt{do}\ P_{\mathit{body}}\ \mathtt{exit}\ P_{\mathit{exit}}: an owned loop in which BB decides whether another iteration of P𝑏𝑜𝑑𝑦P_{\mathit{body}} is executed or whether control exits through P𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡P_{\mathit{exit}}. Again, the body and exit programs may involve multiple lifelines.

3.2 Semantics

The semantics assigns to each global workflow a set of MSCs, each describing one possible global execution. Figure 1 gives the intended intuition, but it should be read as depicting two MSCs, one for each branch of the conditional shown by the dashed case distinction. In general, an execution is represented by one vertical word per lifeline, together with FIFO-matching edges between sends and receives on each channel. Local actions appear as internal events on a single lifeline, while owned conditionals and loops contribute explicit choice events recording which branch or loop outcome was selected. We now make this precise by defining MSCs as tuples of local words.

Definition 2 (Local Alphabets)

For each lifeline A∈ℒA\in\mathscr{L}, the (infinite) local-word alphabet ΣA\Sigma_{A} contains:

  • •

    send letters 𝚜𝚎𝚗𝚍​A​(x→)→B\mathtt{send}\ A(\vec{x})\to B and receive letters 𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚟​A​(y→)←B\mathtt{recv}\ A(\vec{y})\leftarrow B, where x→\vec{x} and y→\vec{y} range over tuples of constants and variables,

  • •

    local action letters 𝚊𝚌𝚝​A:y→=f⁡(x→)\mathtt{act}\ A:\vec{y}=f(\vec{x}), where x→\vec{x} ranges over tuples of constants and variables and y→\vec{y} over tuples of variables,

  • •

    choice letters 𝗂𝖿⊤​(c​@​A),𝗂𝖿⊥​(c​@​A),𝗐𝗁𝗂𝗅𝖾⊤​(c​@​A),𝗐𝗁𝗂𝗅𝖾⊥​(c​@​A)\mathsf{if}_{\top}(c@A),\mathsf{if}_{\bot}(c@A),\mathsf{while}_{\top}(c@A),\mathsf{while}_{\bot}(c@A) for condition cc.

We let ΣA∗\Sigma_{A}^{*} denote the set of finite words over ΣA\Sigma_{A}, which includes the empty word ε\varepsilon. We use u⋅vu\cdot v or u​vuv for the concatenation of words uu and vv.

Though an MSC will be defined as a tuple of local words, one must also specify which send events are matched with which receive events across each channel. Since our execution model uses FIFO channels, this matching is determined canonically by pairing the first send on a channel with the first receive on that channel, the second send with the second receive, and so on. The next definition extracts this channel-wise FIFO matching from a tuple of local words.

Definition 3 (Tuple FIFO Relations)

Fix a tuple of local words M=(wA)A∈ℒM=(w_{A})_{A\in\mathscr{L}} with wA∈ΣA∗w_{A}\in\Sigma_{A}^{*} for each A∈ℒA\in\mathscr{L}. We write |wA||w_{A}| for the length of wAw_{A} and wA​[j]w_{A}[j] for its jjth symbol (starting at index 1). The event set of MM is

EM={(A,i)∣A∈ℒ, 1≤i≤|wA|}.E_{M}=\{(A,i)\mid A\in\mathscr{L},\ 1\leq i\leq|w_{A}|\}.

For each channel A→BA\to B, define the send-event sequence 𝗌𝗇𝖽A→B​(M)=(s1,…,sm)\mathsf{snd}_{A\to B}(M)=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{m}) where (si)i(s_{i})_{i} are exactly the events (A,j)∈EM(A,j)\in E_{M} such that wA​[j]w_{A}[j] is of the form 𝚜𝚎𝚗𝚍​A​(⋅)→B\mathtt{send}\ A(\cdot)\to B, listed in increasing local index jj. Define analogously the receive-event sequence 𝗋𝖼𝗏B←A​(M)=(r1,…,rn)\mathsf{rcv}_{B\leftarrow A}(M)=(r_{1},\ldots,r_{n}) where (ri)i(r_{i})_{i} are exactly the events (B,j)∈EM(B,j)\in E_{M} such that wB​[j]w_{B}[j] is of the form 𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚟​B​(⋅)←A\mathtt{recv}\ B(\cdot)\leftarrow A, again listed in increasing local index.

The FIFO relation ⊲M⊆EM×EM\lhd_{M}\subseteq E_{M}\times E_{M} contains, for each channel A→BA\to B, the pairs (si,ri)(s_{i},r_{i}) for all 1≤i≤min⁡{m,n}1\leq i\leq\min\{m,n\}.

Definition 4 (Payload Matching)

Let x→\vec{x} be a sender payload tuple and let y→\vec{y} be a receiver payload tuple, whose components may be variables or constants. We write 𝗆𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁⁡(x→,y→)\mathsf{match}(\vec{x},\vec{y}) if the following hold:

  1. (1)

    |x→|=|y→||\vec{x}|=|\vec{y}|;

  2. (2)

    for each index ii: if yiy_{i} is a constant, then xix_{i} is the same constant; if yiy_{i} is a variable of type τ\tau, then xix_{i} is either a constant of type τ\tau or a variable of type τ\tau.

Applied to a source-level 𝚖𝚜𝚐​A​(x→)→B⁡(y→)\mathtt{msg}\ A(\vec{x})\to B(\vec{y}), this condition is checked statically as part of well-typedness (see Definition 5 below). When yiy_{i} is a constant, the distributed implementation can additionally verify at runtime that the received value equals that constant, raising an error if not (a lightweight consistency check requiring no extra specification). The same conditions also describe runtime payload agreement for the control-tag payloads introduced later by the projection.

Payload matching isolates the only place where sender and receiver payloads are allowed to differ syntactically: receivers may bind variables or require distinguished constants. The raw workflow grammar itself does not enforce that messages match in this sense, nor that actions and guards are locally consistent. We therefore restrict attention to a well-typed fragment.

Definition 5 (Well-Typed Global Workflows)

A global workflow PP is well typed if all the following conditions hold:

  1. (1)

    every message subprogram 𝚖𝚜𝚐​A​(x→)→B⁡(y→)\mathtt{msg}\ A(\vec{x})\to B(\vec{y}) satisfies 𝗆𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁⁡(x→,y→)\mathsf{match}(\vec{x},\vec{y});

  2. (2)

    every action subprogram 𝚊𝚌𝚝​A:y→=f⁡(x→)\mathtt{act}\ A:\vec{y}=f(\vec{x}) is locally type-correct, i.e., the invocation f⁡(x→)f(\vec{x}) is assumed to produce values compatible with the variables y→\vec{y};

  3. (3)

    every control condition c​@​Bc@B occurring in an 𝚒𝚏\mathtt{if} or 𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎\mathtt{while} statement is well typed for lifeline BB, i.e., cc is a Boolean expression over variables available at BB.

Throughout the remainder of the paper, we consider only well-typed global workflows.

In fact, only item (1) is needed to ensure that the inductive MSC semantics below is well defined. Items (2)–(3) record additional static consistency conditions expected of executable programs, but are not used explicitly in the semantic constructions below.

We can now say which tuples of local words actually represent executions. Intuitively, a valid MSC must have every receive matched by a send, matched events must agree on their payloads, and the causal dependencies induced by local order and communication must not form cycles.

Definition 6 (MSC)

An MSC is a tuple of local words M=(wA)A∈ℒM=(w_{A})_{A\in\mathscr{L}} with wA∈ΣA∗w_{A}\in\Sigma_{A}^{*} such that:

  1. (1)

    every receive event in wAw_{A} is matched in ⊲M\lhd_{M};

  2. (2)

    whenever a send event with payload tuple x→\vec{x} is matched to a receive event with payload tuple y→\vec{y}, they satisfy 𝗆𝖺𝗍𝖼𝗁⁡(x→,y→)\mathsf{match}(\vec{x},\vec{y}) (in particular, receiver constants are matched by value equality);

  3. (3)

    the transitive closure of the binary relation ⊲M∪{((A,i),(A,i+1))∣A∈ℒ,i∈{1,…,|wA|−1}}{\lhd_{M}}\cup\{((A,i),(A,i+1))\mid A\in\mathscr{L},\,i\in\{1,\ldots,|w_{A}|-1\}\} is a strict partial order (i.e., acyclic).

We call MM complete if every send event is matched in ⊲M\lhd_{M}.

To compose executions sequentially, we use componentwise concatenation: M1∘M2=(uA​vA)A∈ℒM_{1}\circ M_{2}=(u_{A}v_{A})_{A\in\mathscr{L}} for M1=(uA)A,M2=(vA)AM_{1}=(u_{A})_{A},\ M_{2}=(v_{A})_{A}.

The concatenation of two MSCs is not necessarily an MSC. However, we have the following closure facts:

Lemma 1 (Concatenation with a Complete Prefix)

Let M1M_{1} be a complete MSC and M2M_{2} be an MSC. Then M1∘M2M_{1}\circ M_{2} is an MSC. If moreover M2M_{2} is complete, then M1∘M2M_{1}\circ M_{2} is complete.

Lemma 2 (Stripping a Complete Prefix)

Conversely, let C=(uA)AC=(u_{A})_{A} be a complete MSC and let N=(vA)AN=(v_{A})_{A} be a tuple of local words. If C∘N=(uA​vA)AC\circ N=(u_{A}v_{A})_{A} is an MSC, then NN is an MSC. If C∘NC\circ N is a complete MSC, then NN is a complete MSC.

With these ingredients in place, the semantics can be defined compositionally. The base cases are canonical one-step MSCs for the atomic workflow constructs. Sequential composition uses concatenation of MSCs, and owned conditionals and loops contribute explicit choice events on the deciding lifeline.

Definition 7 (Canonical MSCs)

Fix A,B∈ℒA,B\in\mathscr{L}, tuples x→,y→\vec{x},\vec{y}, action f∈ℱf\in\mathscr{F}, and choice letter γ∈{𝗂𝖿⊤​(c​@​B),𝗂𝖿⊥​(c​@​B),𝗐𝗁𝗂𝗅𝖾⊤​(c​@​B),𝗐𝗁𝗂𝗅𝖾⊥​(c​@​B)}\gamma\in\{\mathsf{if}_{\top}(c@B),\mathsf{if}_{\bot}(c@B),\mathsf{while}_{\top}(c@B),\mathsf{while}_{\bot}(c@B)\} for some condition cc. We define the following canonical MSCs:

  • •

    MεM_{\varepsilon} is the MSC with no events on any lifeline;

  • •

    MγB=(wX)X∈ℒM_{\gamma}^{B}=(w_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}}, where wB=γw_{B}=\gamma and wX=ε⁡(X≠B)w_{X}=\varepsilon~(X\neq B);

  • •

    Mx→,y→A,f=(wX)X∈ℒM_{\vec{x},\vec{y}}^{A,f}=(w_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}}, where wA=𝚊𝚌𝚝​A:y→=f⁡(x→)w_{A}=\mathtt{act}\ A:\vec{y}=f(\vec{x}) and wX=ε⁡(X≠A)w_{X}=\varepsilon~(X\neq A);

  • •

    Mx→,y→A→B=(wX)X∈ℒM_{\vec{x},\vec{y}}^{A\to B}=(w_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}}, where wA=𝚜𝚎𝚗𝚍​A​(x→)→Bw_{A}=\mathtt{send}\ A(\vec{x})\to B, wB=𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚟​B​(y→)←Aw_{B}=\mathtt{recv}\ B(\vec{y})\leftarrow A, and wX=ε⁡(X∉{A,B})w_{X}=\varepsilon~(X\notin\{A,B\}).

Definition 8 (Inductive MSC Semantics)

The semantics ⟦P⟧\llbracket P\rrbracket of a well-typed global workflow PP is a set of MSCs. It is defined by structural recursion with the rules given in Table 1.

One observes that for every well-typed global workflow PP and every M∈⟦P⟧M\in\llbracket P\rrbracket, the MSC MM is complete. This follows by structural induction on PP from the semantic clauses.

4 Distributed Agent Programs

A distributed agent program assigns one local program to each lifeline. The local program at A∈ℒA\in\mathscr{L} describes the steps visible at AA: sends and receives on AA’s channels, local actions, and control steps arising from branching decisions that AA either owns or observes via a received control signal.

Definition 9 (Local Syntax)

For each lifeline A∈ℒA\in\mathscr{L}, let 𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗀A\mathsf{LocProg}_{A} be the set of local programs at AA, generated by the grammar

S::=\displaystyle S::={} ε∣𝚜𝚎𝚗𝚍A(x→)→B∣𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚟A(y→)←B∣𝚊𝚌𝚝A:y→=f(x→)∣S1;S2∣\displaystyle\varepsilon\mid\mathtt{send}\ A(\vec{x})\to B\mid\mathtt{recv}\ A(\vec{y})\leftarrow B\mid\mathtt{act}\ A:\vec{y}=f(\vec{x})\mid S_{1};S_{2}\mid
𝚒𝚏c@A𝚝𝚑𝚎𝚗S⊤𝚎𝚕𝚜𝚎S⊥∣𝚒𝚏A(y→)←B𝚝𝚑𝚎𝚗S⊤𝚎𝚕𝚜𝚎S⊥∣\displaystyle\mathtt{if}\ c@A\ \mathtt{then}\ S_{\top}\ \mathtt{else}\ S_{\bot}\mid\mathtt{if}\ A(\vec{y})\leftarrow B\ \mathtt{then}\ S_{\top}\ \mathtt{else}\ S_{\bot}\mid
𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎​c​@​A​𝚍𝚘​S𝑏𝑜𝑑𝑦​𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝​S𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡|𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎​A​(y→)←B​𝚍𝚘​S𝑏𝑜𝑑𝑦​𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝​S𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡\displaystyle\mathtt{while}\ c@A\ \mathtt{do}\ S_{\mathit{body}}\ \mathtt{exit}\ S_{\mathit{exit}}\mid\mathtt{while}\ A(\vec{y})\leftarrow B\ \mathtt{do}\ S_{\mathit{body}}\ \mathtt{exit}\ S_{\mathit{exit}}

where cc ranges over source guards. Here, each occurrence of BB ranges over lifelines in ℒ∖{A}\mathscr{L}\setminus\{A\}. In 𝚜𝚎𝚗𝚍​A​(x→)→B\mathtt{send}\ A(\vec{x})\to B and 𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚟​A​(y→)←B\mathtt{recv}\ A(\vec{y})\leftarrow B, x→\vec{x} and y→\vec{y} range over tuples of constants and variables. In action statements, y→\vec{y} must be variables (assignment targets). For constructs 𝚒𝚏/𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎​A​(y→)←B\mathtt{if}/\mathtt{while}\ A(\vec{y})\leftarrow B, y→\vec{y} is a non-empty tuple of constants and variables whose first component y1y_{1} is a Boolean variable.

Definition 10 (Distributed Programs)

A distributed program is a tuple 𝒟=(SA)A∈ℒ\mathcal{D}=(S_{A})_{A\in\mathscr{L}} with SA∈𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗀AS_{A}\in\mathsf{LocProg}_{A} for each AA.

The message and action constructs are the local counterparts of the corresponding workflow constructs, as are the owner-side conditional control-flow constructs 𝚒𝚏​c​@​A\mathtt{if}\ c@A and 𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎​c​@​A\mathtt{while}\ c@A: they still represent source-level local control owned by AA. The receive-guarded forms 𝚒𝚏/𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎​A​(y→)←B\mathtt{if}/\mathtt{while}\ A(\vec{y})\leftarrow B are different: they do not evaluate a guard locally, but instead react to a control decision that has already been made by BB and communicated explicitly.

The semantics of a local program is a language of local traces, one word over the alphabet ΣA\Sigma_{A} from Definition 2 for each possible execution of lifeline AA. The semantics of a distributed program then contains the tuples of such local traces that together form an MSC. In this way, the distributed semantics reuses the MSC notion from Section 3, but starts from already projected local behavior rather than from a global workflow directly.

For S∈𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗀AS\in\mathsf{LocProg}_{A}, we define ⟨⟨S⟩⟩⊆ΣA∗{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}\subseteq\Sigma_{A}^{*}, the set of local traces of SS, by induction. The receive-guarded control constructs 𝚒𝚏/𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎​A​(y→)←B\mathtt{if}/\mathtt{while}\ A(\vec{y})\leftarrow B consume control-tagged messages from BB and branch on the first component (⊤\top or ⊥\bot). The formal definition is given in Table 2; there, we write y→​[ν/y1]\vec{y}[\nu/y_{1}] for the tuple obtained by replacing y1y_{1} by ν\nu.

To reason about partial executions and to formalize deadlock-freeness, we order local words and MSC tuples by the componentwise prefix relation. For words u,u′∈ΣA∗u,u^{\prime}\in\Sigma_{A}^{*}, write u⪯u′u\preceq u^{\prime} if there is v∈ΣA∗v\in\Sigma_{A}^{*} such that u′=u​vu^{\prime}=uv. We write u≺u′u\prec u^{\prime} if u⪯u′u\preceq u^{\prime} and u≠u′u\neq u^{\prime}.

A language L⊆ΣA∗L\subseteq\Sigma_{A}^{*} is called prefix-free if no two distinct words in LL are prefix-comparable.

Lemma 3 (Complete Local Traces Are Prefix-Free)

For every local program S∈𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗀AS\in\mathsf{LocProg}_{A}, the language ⟨⟨S⟩⟩{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} is prefix-free.

Now that we have defined the local trace languages, the semantics of a distributed program is obtained by considering the tuples with one local trace for each lifeline, and keeping exactly those tuples that satisfy the MSC conditions from Definition 6. We define two semantics for distributed programs: one for complete executions and one for partial executions, where each local trace may be a prefix of a complete one.

Given a distributed program 𝒟=(SA)A∈ℒ\mathcal{D}=(S_{A})_{A\in\mathscr{L}}, its complete MSC semantics is

⟦𝒟⟧={M=(wA)A∈ℒ|wA∈⟨⟨SA⟩⟩​for all ​A,M​is a complete MSC}.\llbracket\mathcal{D}\rrbracket=\left\{M=(w_{A})_{A\in\mathscr{L}}\ \middle|\ \begin{array}[]{l}w_{A}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S_{A}{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}\ \text{for all }A,\\ M\ \text{is a complete MSC}\end{array}\right\}.

For S∈𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗀AS\in\mathsf{LocProg}_{A}, we consider the prefix closure ⟨⟨S⟩⟩𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿⊆ΣA∗{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}_{\mathsf{pref}}\subseteq\Sigma_{A}^{*}, defined as ⟨⟨S⟩⟩𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿={u∈ΣA∗∣∃v∈⟨⟨S⟩⟩:u⪯v}{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}_{\mathsf{pref}}=\{u\in\Sigma_{A}^{*}\mid\exists v\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}\colon u\preceq v\}. The distributed prefix semantics is

⟦𝒟⟧𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿={M=(wA)A∈ℒ|wA∈⟨⟨SA⟩⟩𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿​for all ​A,M​is an MSC}.\llbracket\mathcal{D}\rrbracket_{\mathsf{pref}}=\left\{M=(w_{A})_{A\in\mathscr{L}}\ \middle|\ \begin{array}[]{l}w_{A}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S_{A}{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}_{\mathsf{pref}}\ \text{for all }A,\\ M\ \text{is an MSC}\end{array}\right\}.

Clearly, ⟦𝒟⟧⊆⟦𝒟⟧𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿\llbracket\mathcal{D}\rrbracket\subseteq\llbracket\mathcal{D}\rrbracket_{\mathsf{pref}}. In particular, ⟦𝒟⟧\llbracket\mathcal{D}\rrbracket contains only complete MSCs (hence MSCs) by Definition 6. Note that MSC-ness is defined directly on tuples of local words, independently of any global workflow.

For tuples M=(wA)A∈ℒM=(w_{A})_{A\in\mathscr{L}} and M′=(wA′)A∈ℒM^{\prime}=(w^{\prime}_{A})_{A\in\mathscr{L}}, define M⪯M′M\preceq M^{\prime} if, for all A∈ℒA\in\mathscr{L}, we have wA⪯wA′w_{A}\preceq w^{\prime}_{A}.

Definition 11 (Deadlock-Freeness)

A distributed program 𝒟\mathcal{D} is deadlock-free if, for all M∈⟦𝒟⟧𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿M\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}\rrbracket_{\mathsf{pref}}, there is M′∈⟦𝒟⟧M^{\prime}\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}\rrbracket such that M⪯M′M\preceq M^{\prime}.

In a general distributed system, the same prefix MSC can arise from two different branch histories, one completable and one not, so a complete extension need not witness genuine progress. In our framework, prefix-freeness of local trace languages ensures that every prefix uniquely identifies the branch history taken, so a complete extension always witnesses genuine progress, and deadlock-freeness (Definition 11) is a meaningful guarantee.

5 From Global to Distributed Programs

This section explains how a global workflow is turned into a distributed program. We first define the syntax-directed projection itself, and then state its correctness with respect to the MSC semantics.

5.1 Projection

We now pass from global workflows to executable local programs. The projection is syntax-directed: each workflow construct is translated locally for every lifeline, and the resulting local programs together form the distributed program that will be executed. Three ingredients are needed. First, for owned control constructs, the deciding lifeline must know which other lifelines may participate in the continuation. Second, the projected implementation uses explicit control broadcasts that are not present in the global semantics, so we compare projected executions to global ones only after erasing these auxiliary events.

To determine which lifelines may need to observe a control decision, we use a simple structural participation analysis.

Definition 12 (Structural Participation Sets)

For a global workflow PP, the participation set ℒ⁡(P)\mathscr{L}(P) is defined inductively as follows:

ℒ⁡(𝚖𝚜𝚐​A​(x→)→B⁡(y→))\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(\mathtt{msg}\ A(\vec{x})\to B(\vec{y})) ={A,B},ℒ⁡(ε)=∅,\displaystyle=\{A,B\},\qquad\mathscr{L}(\varepsilon)=\varnothing,
ℒ(𝚊𝚌𝚝A:y→=f(x→))\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(\mathtt{act}\ A:\vec{y}=f(\vec{x})) ={A},ℒ⁡(P1,P2)=ℒ⁡(P1)∪ℒ⁡(P2),\displaystyle=\{A\},\qquad\mathscr{L}(P_{1};P_{2})=\mathscr{L}(P_{1})\cup\mathscr{L}(P_{2}),
ℒ⁡(𝚒𝚏​c​@​B​𝚝𝚑𝚎𝚗​P⊤​𝚎𝚕𝚜𝚎​P⊥)\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(\mathtt{if}\ c@B\ \mathtt{then}\ P_{\top}\ \mathtt{else}\ P_{\bot}) ={B}∪ℒ⁡(P⊤)∪ℒ⁡(P⊥),\displaystyle=\{B\}\cup\mathscr{L}(P_{\top})\cup\mathscr{L}(P_{\bot}),
ℒ⁡(𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎​c​@​B​𝚍𝚘​P𝑏𝑜𝑑𝑦​𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝​P𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡)\displaystyle\mathscr{L}(\mathtt{while}\ c@B\ \mathtt{do}\ P_{\mathit{body}}\ \mathtt{exit}\ P_{\mathit{exit}}) ={B}∪ℒ⁡(P𝑏𝑜𝑑𝑦)∪ℒ⁡(P𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡).\displaystyle=\{B\}\cup\mathscr{L}(P_{\mathit{body}})\cup\mathscr{L}(P_{\mathit{exit}}).

Using these sets, projection turns each owned decision into an explicit broadcast from the decider to the lifelines that may continue afterwards. Fix a total order ⊏\sqsubset on lifelines. For R⊆ℒ∖{B}R\subseteq\mathscr{L}\setminus\{B\}, we write ∏A∈R⊏𝚜𝚎𝚗𝚍​B​(ν,κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P)→A∈𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗀B\prod\nolimits_{A\in R}^{\sqsubset}\mathtt{send}\ B(\nu,\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P})\to A\in\mathsf{LocProg}_{B} for the sequence of decision sends in ⊏\sqsubset-order, where ν∈{⊤,⊥}\nu\in\{\top,\bot\} is the decision value and PP is the construct being projected; if R=∅R=\emptyset, the product is the empty program ε\varepsilon. Each control-flow construct PP uses a dedicated control tag κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P} (indexed by that construct), reserved so that source-level user messages never carry it. Two constructs that share a tag must be syntactically equal and therefore cannot be nested inside each other. Thus, control messages of nested constructs always carry distinct tags and are syntactically distinguishable.

These control broadcasts are implementation details: they are needed to realize owned control in distributed code, but they should not appear in the global workflow semantics. We therefore compare projected executions to global executions only after erasing them. For each lifeline AA, let 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾A:ΣA∗→ΣA∗\mathsf{erase}_{A}:\Sigma_{A}^{*}\to\Sigma_{A}^{*} delete all decision-broadcast send/receive letters introduced by projection for control constructs (the 𝚜𝚎𝚗𝚍B(⊤/⊥,κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P)→A\mathtt{send}\ B(\top/\bot,\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P})\to A and 𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚟A(⊤/⊥,κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P)←B\mathtt{recv}\ A(\top/\bot,\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P})\leftarrow B events, for any control construct PP, used only for control decisions). For an MSC M=(wA)AM=(w_{A})_{A}, define 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾⁡(M)=(𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾A​(wA))A∈ℒ.\mathsf{erase}(M)=(\mathsf{erase}_{A}(w_{A}))_{A\in\mathscr{L}}.

Lemma 4 (Erasure Preserves MSC and Completeness)

If MM is an MSC, then 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾⁡(M)\mathsf{erase}(M) is an MSC. If MM is a complete MSC, then 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾⁡(M)\mathsf{erase}(M) is complete.

With these conventions fixed, the projection rules themselves are straightforward. Atomic statements are projected pointwise to the relevant endpoints or owner lifeline. Sequential composition is projected componentwise. The only interesting case is owned control: the owner keeps its source-level if/while, emits explicit control messages, and each recipient branches by receiving a reserved control token from the owner. For each lifeline A∈ℒA\in\mathscr{L}, we define πA:𝖶𝗈𝗋𝗄→𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗀A\pi_{A}\colon\mathsf{Work}\to\mathsf{LocProg}_{A}. The projection rules are given in Tables 3, 4, and 5, where we let ℛ𝑖𝑓=(ℒ⁡(P⊤)∪ℒ⁡(P⊥))∖{B}\mathcal{R}_{\mathit{if}}=(\mathscr{L}(P_{\top})\cup\mathscr{L}(P_{\bot}))\setminus\{B\} and ℛ𝑤ℎ𝑖𝑙𝑒=(ℒ⁡(P𝑏𝑜𝑑𝑦)∪ℒ⁡(P𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡))∖{B}\mathcal{R}_{\mathit{while}}=(\mathscr{L}(P_{\mathit{body}})\cup\mathscr{L}(P_{\mathit{exit}}))\setminus\{B\}. For recipient-side control constructs, (z,κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P)(z,\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P}) is the received payload, where zz is a Boolean variable not occurring in PP and κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P} is the control tag of the enclosing construct PP.

For a global workflow PP, we write 𝒟P=(πA​(P))A∈ℒ\mathcal{D}_{P}=(\pi_{A}(P))_{A\in\mathscr{L}} for its projected distributed program.

Let |P||P| be the number of syntactic nodes of PP and n=|ℒ|n=|\mathscr{L}|. Each global construct contributes at most one local node per lifeline, giving at most n​|P|n|P| nodes overall. Moreover, each control construct adds at most two owner-side broadcast sequences, each of length at most n−1n-1. Hence the total size of all projections is at most n​|P|+2​(n−1)​|P|=O⁡(n​|P|)n|P|+2(n-1)|P|=O(n|P|), and so each individual projection πX​(P)\pi_{X}(P) is also O⁡(n​|P|)O(n|P|).

Two design choices for local control keep the formal layer compact. First, we keep dedicated recipient-side constructs 𝚒𝚏/𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎​A​(z,κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P)←B\mathtt{if}/\mathtt{while}\ A(z,\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P})\leftarrow B rather than rewriting them into plain 𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚟\mathtt{recv} followed by ordinary 𝚒𝚏/𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎\mathtt{if}/\mathtt{while}: this preserves an explicit receive-to-branch coupling without introducing guard evaluation machinery. Second, control broadcasts use constant values ⊤,⊥\top,\bot tagged with the per-construct tag κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P}. Indexing the tag by the construct PP ensures that control messages of distinct nested constructs are syntactically distinguishable, which simplifies the decision-prefix attribution argument in the proof of Lemma 5. The tag also cleanly separates control traffic from user messages and identifies exactly the events removed by the erasure map. In particular, payload matching ensures that a receive expecting (⊤,κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P)(\top,\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P}) cannot match a send carrying (⊥,κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P)(\bot,\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P}), and conversely.

5.2 Correctness

We can now state the main correctness result of the projection. The theorem establishes that global and projected executions agree up to control messages: every global execution is realized by a distributed one after inserting the necessary control broadcasts, and every complete distributed execution yields a global one once control messages are removed.

Theorem 5.1 (Inductive Correctness)

Let PP be a well-typed global workflow. Then the following hold:

  1. (1)

    For every M∈⟦P⟧M\in\llbracket P\rrbracket, there exists M^∈⟦𝒟P⟧\hat{M}\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}_{P}\rrbracket such that 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾⁡(M^)=M\mathsf{erase}(\hat{M})=M.

  2. (2)

    For every M^∈⟦𝒟P⟧\hat{M}\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}_{P}\rrbracket, 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾⁡(M^)∈⟦P⟧\mathsf{erase}(\hat{M})\in\llbracket P\rrbracket.

Our semantics ranges only over finite, complete MSCs and their finite prefixes. Accordingly, Theorem 5.1 is a partial-correctness statement about terminating workflow executions: whenever a global or projected run reaches a complete finite execution, the erasure-based correspondence holds. In particular, every while loop is assumed to terminate, i.e., the owner’s condition eventually becomes false. The theorem is not a separate claim that arbitrary subsymbolic actions terminate, nor does it address infinite reactive behavior. This restriction is appropriate for the protocol workflows considered here. Extending the framework to reactive settings with infinite executions would require a corresponding semantic extension.

Both items are proved by structural induction on PP. Completeness (item 1) is straightforward: each case follows directly by induction. Soundness (item 2) is harder in the sequential composition case: given a distributed execution of P1;P2P_{1};P_{2}, one must show that the P1P_{1}- and P2P_{2}-parts of each local trace together form valid MSCs. The Zipper lemma resolves exactly this difficulty. Deadlock-freeness (Corollary 1) then follows directly: applying the Zipper lemma with empty suffix extends any prefix execution to a complete one.

Definition 13 (Zipper postcondition)

Let PP be a well-typed global workflow, and let U=(uX)X∈ℒU=(u_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}}, U¯=(u¯X)X∈ℒ\bar{U}=(\bar{u}_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}}, and V=(vX)X∈ℒV=(v_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}} be tuples of local words. We write

𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍P​(U,U¯,V)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{P}(U,\bar{U},V)

if the following hold:

  1. (1)

    for every X∈ℒX\in\mathscr{L}, uX⪯u¯Xu_{X}\preceq\bar{u}_{X}, u¯X∈⟨⟨πX​(P)⟩⟩\bar{u}_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}, and (vX≠ε⟹u¯X=uX)(v_{X}\neq\varepsilon~\Longrightarrow~\bar{u}_{X}=u_{X});

  2. (2)

    U¯\bar{U} is a complete MSC;

  3. (3)

    (uX​vX)X∈ℒ(u_{X}v_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}} is an MSC;

  4. (4)

    (u¯X​vX)X∈ℒ(\bar{u}_{X}v_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}} is an MSC.

The key result is that the Zipper postcondition is always satisfiable.

Lemma 5 (Zipper lemma)

Let PP be a well-typed global workflow. Let U=(uX)X∈ℒU=(u_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}} and V=(vX)X∈ℒV=(v_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}} be tuples of local words such that:

  • •

    for every lifeline X∈ℒX\in\mathscr{L}, uX∈⟨⟨πX​(P)⟩⟩𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿u_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}_{\mathsf{pref}};

  • •

    for every lifeline X∈ℒX\in\mathscr{L}, vX≠ε⟹uX∈⟨⟨πX​(P)⟩⟩v_{X}\neq\varepsilon~\Longrightarrow~u_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}.

Define M=(uX​vX)X∈ℒM=(u_{X}v_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}}. If MM is an MSC, then there exists a tuple U¯=(u¯X)X∈ℒ\bar{U}=(\bar{u}_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}} such that

𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍P​(U,U¯,V).\mathsf{ZipPost}_{P}(U,\bar{U},V).

Intuitively, the lemma addresses the key difficulty of asynchronous sequential composition: in an execution of P1;P2P_{1};P_{2}, different lifelines may cross the P1/P2P_{1}/P_{2}-boundary at different times, leaving some still inside P1P_{1} while others have already begun P2P_{2}. The lemma guarantees that P1P_{1} can always be completed consistently with whatever P2P_{2}-work has started. This is the situation illustrated by reviewed_execution.

Three auxiliary consequences of 𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍P​(U,U¯,V)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{P}(U,\bar{U},V) will be used below. First, the prefix tuple UU is itself an MSC. Second, if each component uXu_{X} is already a complete local trace of πX​(P)\pi_{X}(P), then UU is in fact a complete MSC. Third, VV is an MSC: conditions 2 and 4 together with Lemma 2 give this directly, so it need not be imposed separately in the definition. The first two facts are stated formally in Appendix 0.A as Lemma 8, Lemma 9, and Corollary 2.

Corollary 1 (Deadlock-freeness)

For every well-typed global workflow PP, the distributed program 𝒟P\mathcal{D}_{P} is deadlock-free in the sense of Definition 11.

Corollary 1 is a semantic prefix-extension property: every prefix MSC of the projected distributed program can be extended to a complete MSC. This is the no-stuck property formalized in Definition 11. It is not, by itself, a claim about fairness or lock-freedom of every possible runtime scheduler.

5.3 The ZipperGen System

ZipperGen, available at https://zippergen.io, is a Python implementation of the framework described in this paper. Its internal structure follows the formal development step by step. Workflows are written as ordinary Python functions and are decorated with @workflow. The decorator rewrites the function body into an immutable internal representation (IR) whose nodes mirror the formal grammar of Section 3: typed inputs become owned initial variables, message and action statements become message and action nodes, and Python if/while statements with conditions of the form expr @ Lifeline become owned control nodes. LLM and pure actions are declared separately with @llm and @pure. They attach prompts or pure implementations to the symbolic coordination layer, while the workflow itself remains a coordination object.

Execution follows the projected semantics closely. ZipperGen projects the global workflow, spawns one thread per lifeline, and connects lifelines by FIFO queues, one per directed channel. Control broadcasts use per-construct tags κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P}, so they remain disjoint from user traffic and from each other across nested constructs. The LLM backend is pluggable, and a mock backend is available for testing workflows without API access.

ZipperChat, the companion browser UI, streams execution events and renders them as a live MSC-style view. In this way, the prototype does not only implement the formal model, but also displays its executions in essentially the same visual language as the semantics.

Runtime Planning.

The framework as presented treats workflows as static specifications. ZipperGen also supports a @planner decorator for cases where the coordination structure is not known in advance. A planner action is declared like any other action and can be used directly inside a @workflow:

At runtime, ZipperGen builds a hidden system prompt from all of the following: the description, an auto-generated summary of the available workers, DSL rules, and any allow extensions. An optional actions parameter supplies a pre-defined vocabulary. Since every ZipperGen action (@llm, @pure, @planner, or @workflow) presents the same interface of typed inputs and a typed output, any of these may in principle appear in the vocabulary. The planner receives their signatures and may call them directly in the generated workflow. The allow parameter controls what else the generated workflow may use: "pure" and "llm" permit the LLM to define new actions beyond the supplied vocabulary, while "if" and "while" enable conditional branching and loops. By default only linear workflows over the supplied action vocabulary are permitted. The optional instructions parameter lets the user guide how workers are assigned to tasks. Without it the runtime encourages the planner to use as many workers as reasonable.

The designated LLM also receives the actual values of all input variables, so it sees what it is working with rather than just variable names, and generates a complete sub-workflow in the ZipperGen DSL. ZipperGen validates the generated workflow, projects it, and executes it. Worker lifelines are declared by name in @planner and created implicitly for the sub-workflow’s isolated scope, with their own threads and channels. Worker names must be distinct from the calling lifeline, since the caller appears as a participant in the sub-workflow itself. Nested planners work without any additional declaration. Under these conditions the same projection and deadlock-freedom guarantees apply as for handwritten workflows.

Runtime generation does introduce uncertainty: the sub-workflow is LLM-produced and may not behave as intended. Three properties of the framework help manage this. First, each sub-workflow is isolated: it runs within its own lifeline scope and cannot affect the outer workflow except through its declared return value. Second, structural invariants are checked before execution. In particular, the sub-workflow must end with a worker sending the result back to the planner followed by a return, so the boundary with the outer workflow is always explicit. Third, ZipperGen renders each sub-workflow as a separate, inspectable MSC in ZipperChat, making it straightforward to see exactly what the generated workflow did.

6 Example: Medical Diagnosis Consensus

We illustrate the language with a consensus workflow for medical diagnosis (Listing 3). Two independent LLMs analyze patient notes to determine whether a diagnosis (e.g., sepsis) applies. Each makes an independent assessment, then they exchange verdicts and reasoning, iterating until consensus. The loop continues until both agents reach agreement, at which point the final verdict is returned to the user. LLM1 owns the loop and broadcasts the continuation decision to LLM2 at each iteration; deadlock-freedom (Corollary 1) guarantees that every partial execution can be extended to a complete one.

The LLM action definition of assess is shown in Listing 4. The action reconsider is analogous. The remaining actions check_agreement, inc_trials, and choose_result are simple (non-LLM) functions. 𝙻𝙻𝙼𝟷\mathtt{LLM1} owns the loop. Both LLMs appear in the body, so 𝙻𝙻𝙼𝟸\mathtt{LLM2} receives a control broadcast at each iteration to learn whether execution continues or exits. The initial assessments are structurally independent: both LLMs act on the same notes without seeing each other’s reasoning before the first verdict exchange. This independence is visible in the global workflow and requires no additional annotation or runtime enforcement.

Additional executable examples, including a planning-based parallel arithmetic evaluator, are included in the companion ZipperGen artifact.

Verifiable properties.

The workflow is deadlock-free by construction. The control structure bounds the number of reconsideration rounds by max_rounds. This is a bound on the coordination pattern, not a termination guarantee for individual LLM calls. If execution reaches the final result-selection step, the returned value is either the agreed verdict or the conservative fallback unknown.

7 Conclusion

We presented a domain-specific language for multi-agent LLM coordination based on message sequence charts, together with a syntax-directed projection that derives correct local programs from a global workflow specification. The projection is always defined, requires no realizability check, and guarantees deadlock-freedom by construction. The framework further extends to runtime-generated sub-workflows: a planning LLM produces a syntactically valid global workflow, which is then projected and executed with the same correctness guarantees as a statically written program.

Future work includes a formal treatment of stale or non-returning LLM calls, where timeout mechanisms and their semantic consequences will be essential. A second direction is the integration of coregions [16], which relax the total order on receptions within a lifeline and allow a more flexible treatment of concurrency. Finally, the precise operational semantics of the framework makes it a natural setting for runtime verification: monitors can be derived from the global workflow and used to enforce safety properties at the boundary of the non-verifiable LLM components, providing trust guarantees that static analysis alone cannot offer. Recent work on trace-based assurance for agentic systems [23] illustrates the kind of runtime contracts and failure classes that such monitors could target.

Appendix 0.A Proofs

0.A.1 Proof of Lemma 1 (Concatenation with a Complete Prefix)

For the MSC part, consider M1=(uA)AM_{1}=(u_{A})_{A} complete and M2=(vA)AM_{2}=(v_{A})_{A} an MSC. Every receive event of M1∘M2M_{1}\circ M_{2} lies either in the prefix M1M_{1} or in the suffix M2M_{2}. Prefix receives are matched inside M1M_{1} because M1M_{1} is complete. Suffix receives are matched inside M2M_{2} because M2M_{2} is an MSC. Hence FIFO matching is defined on M1∘M2M_{1}\circ M_{2}, and label compatibility is inherited componentwise from M1M_{1} and M2M_{2}.

For acyclicity, note that all cross-component causality edges go from events of M1M_{1} to events of M2M_{2}: local successor edges cross the concatenation boundary only in that direction, and message-matching edges cannot point from M2M_{2} back into M1M_{1} because every send in M1M_{1} is already matched inside the complete prefix M1M_{1}. Thus a cycle in M1∘M2M_{1}\circ M_{2} would restrict to a cycle in M1M_{1} or M2M_{2}, impossible since both are MSCs. Therefore M1∘M2M_{1}\circ M_{2} is an MSC.

If M2M_{2} is complete as well, then every send in the concatenation is matched inside its own factor, so M1∘M2M_{1}\circ M_{2} is complete. ∎

0.A.2 Proof of Lemma 2 (Stripping a Complete Prefix)

For the MSC part, every receive event occurring in the suffix NN is matched in C∘NC\circ N. Because CC is complete, no such suffix receive can be matched to a send from the prefix CC. Otherwise, the corresponding channel would have an unmatched send in CC. Hence all suffix receives are matched by suffix sends, so FIFO matching is defined on NN. Label compatibility is inherited from C∘NC\circ N. Acyclicity is preserved because the causality relation of NN is the restriction of the causality relation of C∘NC\circ N to suffix events.

If C∘NC\circ N is complete, then every suffix send is matched in C∘NC\circ N. Again, because CC is complete, a suffix send cannot be matched to a receive in the prefix CC. Therefore every suffix send is matched inside NN, so NN is complete.

0.A.3 Proof of Lemma 3

By structural induction on SS. The atomic cases are singletons and therefore prefix-free.

For sequential composition, let

u​v,u′​v′∈⟨⟨S1;S2⟩⟩uv,\ u^{\prime}v^{\prime}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S_{1};S_{2}{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}

with u,u′∈⟨⟨S1⟩⟩u,u^{\prime}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S_{1}{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} and v,v′∈⟨⟨S2⟩⟩v,v^{\prime}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S_{2}{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}, and assume u​v⪯u′​v′uv\preceq u^{\prime}v^{\prime}. Then uu and u′u^{\prime} are both prefixes of the word u′​v′u^{\prime}v^{\prime}, hence they are comparable by ⪯\preceq. By IH on S1S_{1}, the language ⟨⟨S1⟩⟩{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S_{1}{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} is prefix-free, so u=u′u=u^{\prime}. It follows that v⪯v′v\preceq v^{\prime}, and IH on S2S_{2} gives v=v′v=v^{\prime}. Thus u​v=u′​v′uv=u^{\prime}v^{\prime}.

For each control construct, we distinguish two projection cases: the owner case, where the true and false branches begin with distinct choice letters (namely 𝗂𝖿⊤​(c​@​A)\mathsf{if}_{\top}(c@A) versus 𝗂𝖿⊥​(c​@​A)\mathsf{if}_{\bot}(c@A)), and the recipient case, where they begin with distinct receive events (𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚟A(y→[⊤/y1])←B\mathtt{recv}\ A(\vec{y}[\top/y_{1}])\leftarrow B versus 𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚟A(y→[⊥/y1])←B\mathtt{recv}\ A(\vec{y}[\bot/y_{1}])\leftarrow B). In both cases the argument is the same: two traces starting with different initial letters are incomparable by ⪯\preceq, and if they begin with the same letter, prefix-freeness follows from IH on the selected branch.

For the two while-cases, every complete trace has the form

d⊤u1⋯d⊤ukd⊥vd^{\top}u_{1}\cdots d^{\top}u_{k}d^{\bot}v

where d⊤d^{\top} and d⊥d^{\bot} are the corresponding top/bot decision letters, u1,…,uk∈⟨⟨S𝑏𝑜𝑑𝑦⟩⟩u_{1},\ldots,u_{k}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S_{\mathit{body}}{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}, and v∈⟨⟨S𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡⟩⟩v\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S_{\mathit{exit}}{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}. If two such traces have different numbers of top-decisions, then at the first position where the shorter one exits and the longer one continues, one sees a ⊥\bot-decision versus a ⊤\top-decision, so neither word is a prefix of the other. If the numbers of top-decisions agree, compare the body traces one by one. IH on S𝑏𝑜𝑑𝑦S_{\mathit{body}} forces equality of each uiu_{i}, and IH on S𝑒𝑥𝑖𝑡S_{\mathit{exit}} then forces equality of the final exit traces. Hence the complete traces are prefix-free.

0.A.4 Proof of Lemma 4 (Erasure Preserves MSC Structure)

The map 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾\mathsf{erase} deletes only control-broadcast send/receive events introduced by projection and leaves all other local letters unchanged. Therefore the local successor order on the remaining events is preserved.

If MM is an MSC, every receive event that survives erasure was already a non-control receive in MM, and its matching send also survives erasure. Conversely, deleting matched control send/receive pairs cannot create unmatched receives among the remaining events. Label compatibility is inherited from MM, and acyclicity is preserved because 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾⁡(M)\mathsf{erase}(M) is obtained by restricting the causality relation of MM to the surviving events. Hence 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾⁡(M)\mathsf{erase}(M) is an MSC.

If MM is complete, then every surviving send event in 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾⁡(M)\mathsf{erase}(M) was already matched in MM by a surviving receive event, since only control broadcast pairs are deleted. Thus every send in 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾⁡(M)\mathsf{erase}(M) is still matched, so we have that 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾⁡(M)\mathsf{erase}(M) is complete.

0.A.5 Boundary-Aligned Sequential Factorization

Lemma 6 (Boundary-aligned sequential factorization)

Let A∈ℒA\in\mathscr{L}, let S1,S2∈𝖫𝗈𝖼𝖯𝗋𝗈𝗀AS_{1},S_{2}\in\mathsf{LocProg}_{A} be local programs at lifeline AA, and let u∈⟨⟨S1;S2⟩⟩𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿u\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S_{1};S_{2}{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}_{\mathsf{pref}}. Then there exist words u1,u2∈ΣA∗u_{1},u_{2}\in\Sigma_{A}^{*} such that

u=u1​u2,u1∈⟨⟨S1⟩⟩𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿,u2∈⟨⟨S2⟩⟩𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿,u=u_{1}u_{2},\qquad u_{1}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S_{1}{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}_{\mathsf{pref}},\qquad u_{2}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S_{2}{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}_{\mathsf{pref}},

and, moreover,

u2≠ε⟹u1∈⟨⟨S1⟩⟩.u_{2}\neq\varepsilon~\Longrightarrow~u_{1}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}S_{1}{\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}.
Proof (Proof of Lemma 6)

Auxiliary notation (decision prefixes).

Let PP be a control construct (if or while) with decider BB, and fix a branch value ν∈{⊤,⊥}\nu\in\{\top,\bot\}. Let ℛ\mathcal{R} be the recipient set of that construct. Write γBν\gamma_{B}^{\nu} for the choice letter that BB emits when it decides ν\nu: this is 𝗂𝖿⊤​(c​@​B)\mathsf{if}_{\top}(c@B) (resp. 𝗂𝖿⊥​(c​@​B)\mathsf{if}_{\bot}(c@B)) for an if-construct, and 𝗐𝗁𝗂𝗅𝖾⊤​(c​@​B)\mathsf{while}_{\top}(c@B) (resp. 𝗐𝗁𝗂𝗅𝖾⊥​(c​@​B)\mathsf{while}_{\bot}(c@B)) for a while-construct. Note that the owner’s component now starts with the choice letter γBν\gamma_{B}^{\nu}, which records the branch taken before any control message is sent. In the if-case, this ensures the decomposition πB​(P)=dBν;πB​(Qν)\pi_{B}(P)=d_{B}^{\nu};\pi_{B}(Q_{\nu}) holds on the decider lifeline, where QνQ_{\nu} denotes the branch subprogram of PP corresponding to ν\nu. Let PP be a projected if- or while-construct with decision-prefix tuple Dν=(dXν)XD^{\nu}=(d_{X}^{\nu})_{X} for some ν∈{⊤,⊥}\nu\in\{\top,\bot\}. Let M=(wX)XM=(w_{X})_{X} be an MSC such that, for every lifeline XX,

for some word sXs_{X}. Define

rX={εif ​wX≺dXν,sXif ​wX=dXν​sX,M′=(rX)X.r_{X}=\begin{cases}\varepsilon&\text{if }w_{X}\prec d_{X}^{\nu},\\ s_{X}&\text{if }w_{X}=d_{X}^{\nu}s_{X},\end{cases}\qquad M^{\prime}=(r_{X})_{X}.

Proof (Proof of Lemma 7)

The deleted events on each lifeline form an initial segment of the decision-prefix block dXνd_{X}^{\nu}.

We check that no unmatched receive is created. Consider a control channel B→AB\to A (owner to recipient). The owner’s send 𝚜𝚎𝚗𝚍​B​(ν,κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P)→A\mathtt{send}\ B(\nu,\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P})\to A appears in dBνd_{B}^{\nu}, and the recipient’s matching receive 𝚛𝚎𝚌𝚟​A​(ν,κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P)←B\mathtt{recv}\ A(\nu,\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P})\leftarrow B is the sole event of dAνd_{A}^{\nu}. If the send is present in wBw_{B}, it lies in dBνd_{B}^{\nu} and is absent from rBr_{B}. The receive is either also present in wAw_{A} (so wA=dAν​tAw_{A}=d_{A}^{\nu}t_{A} and it is likewise absent from rAr_{A}), or absent from wAw_{A} entirely. In both sub-cases no unmatched receive appears in M′M^{\prime}. If the send is absent (wB≺dBνw_{B}\prec d_{B}^{\nu}), then MM being an MSC ensures the receive is absent from wAw_{A} as well (otherwise it would be unmatched in MM), so nothing changes for AA. In all cases no unmatched receive is introduced. Since dXνd_{X}^{\nu} consists entirely of control events (the choice letter and control sends/receives), non-control events appear only in the suffix sXs_{X} and are fully preserved in M′M^{\prime}, hence no unmatched receive or send is introduced on non-control channels either. Label compatibility holds because M′M^{\prime} retains a subset of MM’s events with the same labels. Acyclicity of the happens-before order is preserved because any cycle in M′M^{\prime} would be a cycle in MM, contradicting MM being an MSC. Hence M′M^{\prime} is an MSC. ∎

Recall that mm counts the length of the maximal common visible prefix ν1​…​νm\nu_{1}\ldots\nu_{m} of decision-prefix events of this particular while-construct in MM, where ν1=⊤\nu_{1}=\top in the present subcase. Conversely, its length is at most m−1m-1, because the initial ⊤\top-decision block is no longer present in M′′M^{\prime\prime} and no new decision-prefix events are introduced by either transformation. Therefore the secondary induction measure of M′′M^{\prime\prime} is exactly m−1m-1.

Assume vX≠εv_{X}\neq\varepsilon. Since vX≠εv_{X}\neq\varepsilon implies uX(2)​vX≠εu_{X}^{(2)}v_{X}\neq\varepsilon, the first side condition gives uX(1)∈⟨⟨πX​(Q1)⟩⟩u_{X}^{(1)}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q_{1}){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}. The zipper hypothesis gives uX=uX(1)​uX(2)∈⟨⟨πX​(Q1,Q2)⟩⟩=⟨⟨πX​(Q1)⟩⟩⋅⟨⟨πX​(Q2)⟩⟩u_{X}=u_{X}^{(1)}u_{X}^{(2)}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q_{1};Q_{2}){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}={\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q_{1}){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}\cdot{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q_{2}){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}, so there exist w1′∈⟨⟨πX​(Q1)⟩⟩w_{1}^{\prime}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q_{1}){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} and w2′∈⟨⟨πX​(Q2)⟩⟩w_{2}^{\prime}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q_{2}){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} with uX(1)​uX(2)=w1′​w2′u_{X}^{(1)}u_{X}^{(2)}=w_{1}^{\prime}w_{2}^{\prime}. From uX(1)​uX(2)=w1′​w2′u_{X}^{(1)}u_{X}^{(2)}=w_{1}^{\prime}w_{2}^{\prime}, one of w1′⪯uX(1)w_{1}^{\prime}\preceq u_{X}^{(1)} or uX(1)⪯w1′u_{X}^{(1)}\preceq w_{1}^{\prime} holds (possibly both, when w1′=uX(1)w_{1}^{\prime}=u_{X}^{(1)}). Since both uX(1)u_{X}^{(1)} and w1′w_{1}^{\prime} lie in ⟨⟨πX​(Q1)⟩⟩{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q_{1}){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}, prefix-freeness forces w1′=uX(1)w_{1}^{\prime}=u_{X}^{(1)}, hence uX(2)=w2′∈⟨⟨πX​(Q2)⟩⟩u_{X}^{(2)}=w_{2}^{\prime}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q_{2}){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}.

Write U(1)=(uX(1))XU^{(1)}=(u_{X}^{(1)})_{X} and W=(uX(2)​vX)XW=(u_{X}^{(2)}v_{X})_{X}. Apply IH to Q1Q_{1} and M=(uX(1)​(uX(2)​vX))XM=(u_{X}^{(1)}(u_{X}^{(2)}v_{X}))_{X}. This yields 𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍Q1​(U(1),U¯(1),W)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{Q_{1}}(U^{(1)},\bar{U}^{(1)},W). In particular, WW is an MSC by conditions 2 and 4 of 𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍Q1\mathsf{ZipPost}_{Q_{1}} and Lemma 2. For the second IH application, assume vX≠εv_{X}\neq\varepsilon. Then uX(2)∈⟨⟨πX​(Q2)⟩⟩u_{X}^{(2)}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q_{2}){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} by the boundary-aligned choice above. So the side condition for IH on Q2Q_{2} holds. Apply IH to Q2Q_{2} and WW. This yields 𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍Q2​(U(2),U¯(2),V)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{Q_{2}}(U^{(2)},\bar{U}^{(2)},V). Setting

u¯X=u¯X(1)​u¯X(2)\bar{u}_{X}=\bar{u}_{X}^{(1)}\bar{u}_{X}^{(2)}

gives the required completion for PP. Let U¯=(u¯X)X\bar{U}=(\bar{u}_{X})_{X}. Completeness of U¯\bar{U} follows from completeness of the factors and Lemma 1. Moreover, since U¯(1)\bar{U}^{(1)} is a complete MSC and (u¯X(2)​vX)X(\bar{u}_{X}^{(2)}v_{X})_{X} is an MSC, Lemma 1 yields that (u¯X​vX)X(\bar{u}_{X}v_{X})_{X} is an MSC. Therefore for every XX, uX⪯u¯Xu_{X}\preceq\bar{u}_{X}: the second IH gives uX(2)⪯u¯X(2)u_{X}^{(2)}\preceq\bar{u}_{X}^{(2)} unconditionally; when uX(2)​vX≠εu_{X}^{(2)}v_{X}\neq\varepsilon, the first IH additionally gives u¯X(1)=uX(1)\bar{u}_{X}^{(1)}=u_{X}^{(1)}, so uX=uX(1)​uX(2)⪯uX(1)​u¯X(2)=u¯X(1)​u¯X(2)=u¯Xu_{X}=u_{X}^{(1)}u_{X}^{(2)}\preceq u_{X}^{(1)}\bar{u}_{X}^{(2)}=\bar{u}_{X}^{(1)}\bar{u}_{X}^{(2)}=\bar{u}_{X}; when uX(2)=εu_{X}^{(2)}=\varepsilon and vX=εv_{X}=\varepsilon, the first IH gives uX=uX(1)⪯u¯X(1)⪯u¯Xu_{X}=u_{X}^{(1)}\preceq\bar{u}_{X}^{(1)}\preceq\bar{u}_{X}. Moreover, if vX≠εv_{X}\neq\varepsilon, then u¯X(2)=uX(2)\bar{u}_{X}^{(2)}=u_{X}^{(2)} (second IH) and uX(2)​vX≠εu_{X}^{(2)}v_{X}\neq\varepsilon, so u¯X(1)=uX(1)\bar{u}_{X}^{(1)}=u_{X}^{(1)} (first IH), hence u¯X=uX\bar{u}_{X}=u_{X}. Thus Condition 1 of 𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍Q1;Q2​(U,U¯,V)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{Q_{1};Q_{2}}(U,\bar{U},V) holds, and

𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍Q1;Q2​(U,U¯,V)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{Q_{1};Q_{2}}(U,\bar{U},V)

holds.

0.A.7 Auxiliary Consequences of ZipPost

Lemma 8

If 𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍P​(U,U¯,V)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{P}(U,\bar{U},V) holds, then UU is an MSC.

Proof (Proof of Lemma 8)

Acyclicity and label compatibility are inherited from (uX​vX)X(u_{X}v_{X})_{X} (an MSC by Condition 3 of 𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍P​(U,U¯,V)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{P}(U,\bar{U},V)) by restriction to prefix events.

For the receive-matching condition, suppose that on some channel A→BA\to B, the prefix uBu_{B} contains more receives than uAu_{A} contains sends. Since U¯\bar{U} is a complete MSC (Condition 2), the completion u¯A\bar{u}_{A} must contain an additional send on that channel, hence u¯A≠uA\bar{u}_{A}\neq u_{A}. By Condition 1, this implies vA=εv_{A}=\varepsilon, so the full word for AA in (uX​vX)X(u_{X}v_{X})_{X} is just uAu_{A}. But then (uX​vX)X(u_{X}v_{X})_{X} has an unmatched receive on channel A→BA\to B, contradicting Condition 3. Hence UU has no unmatched receives and is therefore an MSC. ∎

Lemma 9

Let PP be a well-typed global workflow, and let M=(uX)X∈ℒM=(u_{X})_{X\in\mathscr{L}} be a tuple such that

uX∈⟨⟨πX​(P)⟩⟩for every ​X∈ℒ.u_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}\qquad\text{for every }X\in\mathscr{L}.

If MM is an MSC, then MM is a complete MSC.

Proof (Proof of Lemma 9)

Apply Lemma 5 with U=(uX)XU=(u_{X})_{X} and V=(ε)XV=(\varepsilon)_{X}. Since each uX∈⟨⟨πX​(P)⟩⟩u_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}, one has in particular uX∈⟨⟨πX​(P)⟩⟩𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿u_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}_{\mathsf{pref}}, and because every vXv_{X} is ε\varepsilon, the zipper side condition is vacuous. As M=(uX)XM=(u_{X})_{X} is an MSC by hypothesis, Lemma 5 yields a tuple U¯=(u¯X)X\bar{U}=(\bar{u}_{X})_{X} such that 𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍P​(U,U¯,V)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{P}(U,\bar{U},V) holds.

For every lifeline XX, Condition 1 of 𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍P​(U,U¯,V)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{P}(U,\bar{U},V) gives

uX⪯u¯Xandu¯X∈⟨⟨πX​(P)⟩⟩.u_{X}\preceq\bar{u}_{X}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bar{u}_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}.

Since complete local trace languages are prefix-free by Lemma 3, it follows that uX=u¯Xu_{X}=\bar{u}_{X} for every XX. Hence U=U¯U=\bar{U}. Now Condition 2 of 𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍P​(U,U¯,V)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{P}(U,\bar{U},V) states that U¯\bar{U} is a complete MSC. Therefore we have that M=UM=U is a complete MSC as well. ∎

Corollary 2

If 𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍P​(U,U¯,V)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{P}(U,\bar{U},V) holds and uX∈⟨⟨πX​(P)⟩⟩u_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} for every lifeline XX, then UU is a complete MSC.

Proof (Proof of Corollary 2)

By Lemma 8, the tuple U=(uX)XU=(u_{X})_{X} is an MSC. Since uX∈⟨⟨πX​(P)⟩⟩u_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} for every lifeline XX, Lemma 9 implies that UU is a complete MSC. ∎

0.A.8 Control Decomposition

We use the decision-prefix notation Dν=(dXν)XD^{\nu}=(d_{X}^{\nu})_{X} introduced in the proof of Lemma 5.

Lemma 10 (Control Decomposition)

Let PP be a well-typed global workflow.

  1. (1)

    If

    P=𝚒𝚏​c​@​B​𝚝𝚑𝚎𝚗​Q⊤​𝚎𝚕𝚜𝚎​Q⊥P=\mathtt{if}\ c@B\ \mathtt{then}\ Q_{\top}\ \mathtt{else}\ Q_{\bot}

    and M^∈⟦𝒟P⟧\hat{M}\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}_{P}\rrbracket, then there exist a unique ν∈{⊤,⊥}\nu\in\{\top,\bot\} and an MSC M^ν∈⟦𝒟Qν⟧\hat{M}_{\nu}\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}_{Q_{\nu}}\rrbracket such that

    M^=Dν∘M^ν.\hat{M}=D^{\nu}\circ\hat{M}_{\nu}.
  2. (2)

    If

    P=𝚠𝚑𝚒𝚕𝚎​c​@​B​𝚍𝚘​Q​𝚎𝚡𝚒𝚝​EP=\mathtt{while}\ c@B\ \mathtt{do}\ Q\ \mathtt{exit}\ E

    and M^∈⟦𝒟P⟧\hat{M}\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}_{P}\rrbracket, then there exist k≥0k\geq 0, M^1,…,M^k∈⟦𝒟Q⟧\hat{M}_{1},\ldots,\hat{M}_{k}\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}_{Q}\rrbracket, and M^𝑒𝑥∈⟦𝒟E⟧\hat{M}_{\mathit{ex}}\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}_{E}\rrbracket such that

    M^=(D⊤∘M^1)∘⋯∘(D⊤∘M^k)∘(D⊥∘M^𝑒𝑥).\hat{M}=\bigl(D^{\top}\circ\hat{M}_{1}\bigr)\circ\cdots\circ\bigl(D^{\top}\circ\hat{M}_{k}\bigr)\circ\bigl(D^{\bot}\circ\hat{M}_{\mathit{ex}}\bigr).
Proof (Proof of Lemma 10)

If-case. By Table 4, for every lifeline XX the complete local trace language of πX​(P)\pi_{X}(P) consists of words of the form dXν⋅tXd_{X}^{\nu}\cdot t_{X} with ν∈{⊤,⊥}\nu\in\{\top,\bot\} and tX∈⟨⟨πX​(Qν)⟩⟩t_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q_{\nu}){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}. Hence the XX-component of M^\hat{M} starts with dXνXd_{X}^{\nu_{X}} for some νX\nu_{X}. The value νX\nu_{X} is the same for every XX. By Table 4, the owner BB’s complete local trace begins with a single control broadcast of some ν∈{⊤,⊥}\nu\in\{\top,\bot\} to all recipients. By label compatibility of matched send/receive events (Definition 6) and FIFO ordering on each B→XB\to X control channel, every recipient XX’s component of M^\hat{M} also begins with ν\nu; idle agents have dXν=εd_{X}^{\nu}=\varepsilon. Call this common value ν\nu.

Write the XX-component of M^\hat{M} as dXν⋅tXd_{X}^{\nu}\cdot t_{X} (with tX=εt_{X}=\varepsilon for idle agents where dXν=εd_{X}^{\nu}=\varepsilon) and define M^ν=(tX)X\hat{M}_{\nu}=(t_{X})_{X}, so M^=Dν∘M^ν\hat{M}=D^{\nu}\circ\hat{M}_{\nu}. Since DνD^{\nu} is a complete MSC by construction and M^\hat{M} is a complete MSC, Lemma 2 yields that M^ν\hat{M}_{\nu} is a complete MSC. Each component tX∈⟨⟨πX​(Qν)⟩⟩t_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q_{\nu}){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}, so M^ν∈⟦𝒟Qν⟧\hat{M}_{\nu}\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}_{Q_{\nu}}\rrbracket. Uniqueness of M^ν\hat{M}_{\nu} follows because concatenation with the fixed prefix DνD^{\nu} is injective: if Dν∘N=Dν∘N′D^{\nu}\circ N=D^{\nu}\circ N^{\prime} then N=N′N=N^{\prime}.

While-case. We argue by induction on the number k≥0k\geq 0 of ⊤\top-decision blocks in the owner BB’s component of M^\hat{M}.

Base case k=0k=0. Since k=0k=0, the owner BB’s component begins with dB⊥d_{B}^{\bot} (a ⊥\bot-decision block). By label compatibility (Definition 6) and FIFO ordering on each B→XB\to X control channel, every recipient XX’s component of M^\hat{M} also begins with dX⊥d_{X}^{\bot}; idle agents have dX⊥=εd_{X}^{\bot}=\varepsilon. The tuple D⊥=(dX⊥)XD^{\bot}=(d_{X}^{\bot})_{X} is a complete MSC because the control sends on BB are matched to the corresponding control receives on each recipient by the FIFO matching of M^\hat{M}. By Table 5, every complete local trace of πX​(P)\pi_{X}(P) that starts with a ⊥\bot-decision has the form dX⊥⋅eXd_{X}^{\bot}\cdot e_{X} with eX∈⟨⟨πX​(E)⟩⟩e_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(E){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}. Write the XX-component of M^\hat{M} as dX⊥⋅eXd_{X}^{\bot}\cdot e_{X} (with eX=εe_{X}=\varepsilon for idle agents where dX⊥=εd_{X}^{\bot}=\varepsilon) and define M^𝑒𝑥=(eX)X\hat{M}_{\mathit{ex}}=(e_{X})_{X}, so M^=D⊥∘M^𝑒𝑥\hat{M}=D^{\bot}\circ\hat{M}_{\mathit{ex}}. Since D⊥D^{\bot} is a complete MSC and M^\hat{M} is complete, Lemma 2 yields that M^𝑒𝑥\hat{M}_{\mathit{ex}} is a complete MSC with each eX∈⟨⟨πX​(E)⟩⟩e_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(E){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}, hence M^𝑒𝑥∈⟦𝒟E⟧\hat{M}_{\mathit{ex}}\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}_{E}\rrbracket.

Inductive step k>0k>0. Since k>0k>0, the owner BB’s component begins with dB⊤d_{B}^{\top} (a ⊤\top-decision block). By label compatibility (Definition 6) and FIFO ordering on each B→XB\to X control channel, every recipient XX’s component of M^\hat{M} also begins with dX⊤d_{X}^{\top}; idle agents have dX⊤=εd_{X}^{\top}=\varepsilon. The tuple D⊤=(dX⊤)XD^{\top}=(d_{X}^{\top})_{X} is a complete MSC by the same matching argument. By Table 5, every complete local trace of πX​(P)\pi_{X}(P) that starts with a ⊤\top-decision has the form dX⊤⋅sXd_{X}^{\top}\cdot s_{X} with sX∈⟨⟨πX​(Q,P)⟩⟩s_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q;P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}: after the ⊤\top-decision block the body QQ executes completely, followed by the recursive continuation PP. Write the XX-component of M^\hat{M} as dX⊤⋅sXd_{X}^{\top}\cdot s_{X} (with sX=εs_{X}=\varepsilon for idle agents where dX⊤=εd_{X}^{\top}=\varepsilon) and define N=(sX)XN=(s_{X})_{X}, so M^=D⊤∘N\hat{M}=D^{\top}\circ N. Since D⊤D^{\top} is a complete MSC and M^\hat{M} is complete, Lemma 2 yields that NN is a complete MSC with sX∈⟨⟨πX​(Q,P)⟩⟩s_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q;P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} for every XX.

Since sX∈⟨⟨πX​(Q,P)⟩⟩s_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q;P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}, the semantics of sequential composition gives a factorization sX=bX​wXs_{X}=b_{X}w_{X} with bX∈⟨⟨πX​(Q)⟩⟩b_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} and wX∈⟨⟨πX​(P)⟩⟩w_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}. The factorization is unique by prefix-freeness of ⟨⟨πX​(Q)⟩⟩{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} (Lemma 3).

Apply Lemma 5 to QQ with U=(bX)XU=(b_{X})_{X} and V=(wX)XV=(w_{X})_{X}. The prefix condition bX∈⟨⟨πX​(Q)⟩⟩𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿b_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}_{\mathsf{pref}} holds since bX∈⟨⟨πX​(Q)⟩⟩⊆⟨⟨πX​(Q)⟩⟩𝗉𝗋𝖾𝖿b_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}\subseteq{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}_{\mathsf{pref}}. The zipper side condition wX≠ε⟹bX∈⟨⟨πX​(Q)⟩⟩w_{X}\neq\varepsilon\Longrightarrow b_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} holds trivially since bX∈⟨⟨πX​(Q)⟩⟩b_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} for every XX. The tuple (bX​wX)X=N(b_{X}w_{X})_{X}=N is an MSC by the above. The lemma yields U¯\bar{U} with 𝖹𝗂𝗉𝖯𝗈𝗌𝗍Q​(U,U¯,V)\mathsf{ZipPost}_{Q}(U,\bar{U},V). Since bX∈⟨⟨πX​(Q)⟩⟩b_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(Q){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} for every XX, Corollary 2 gives that M^1=(bX)X\hat{M}_{1}=(b_{X})_{X} is a complete MSC, hence M^1∈⟦𝒟Q⟧\hat{M}_{1}\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}_{Q}\rrbracket.

Since N=M^1∘WN=\hat{M}_{1}\circ W with W=(wX)XW=(w_{X})_{X} and both NN and M^1\hat{M}_{1} complete MSCs, Lemma 2 yields that WW is a complete MSC. For each XX, wX∈⟨⟨πX​(P)⟩⟩w_{X}\in{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{X}(P){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle}, so W∈⟦𝒟P⟧W\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}_{P}\rrbracket. The owner’s component in WW contains exactly k−1k-1 ⊤\top-decision blocks: the first block dB⊤d_{B}^{\top} was consumed in passing from M^\hat{M} to NN, and the BB-component of M^1\hat{M}_{1} lies in ⟨⟨πB​(Q)⟩⟩{\langle\hskip-1.99997pt\langle}\pi_{B}(Q){\rangle\hskip-1.99997pt\rangle} and contains no κ𝖼𝗍𝗋𝗅P\kappa_{\mathsf{ctrl}}^{P}-tagged events. Applying the induction hypothesis to WW yields

W=(D⊤∘M^2)∘⋯∘(D⊤∘M^k)∘(D⊥∘M^𝑒𝑥).W=\bigl(D^{\top}\circ\hat{M}_{2}\bigr)\circ\cdots\circ\bigl(D^{\top}\circ\hat{M}_{k}\bigr)\circ\bigl(D^{\bot}\circ\hat{M}_{\mathit{ex}}\bigr).

Prepending D⊤∘M^1D^{\top}\circ\hat{M}_{1} gives

M^=D⊤∘N=D⊤∘M^1∘W=(D⊤∘M^1)∘⋯∘(D⊤∘M^k)∘(D⊥∘M^𝑒𝑥),\hat{M}=D^{\top}\circ N=D^{\top}\circ\hat{M}_{1}\circ W=\bigl(D^{\top}\circ\hat{M}_{1}\bigr)\circ\cdots\circ\bigl(D^{\top}\circ\hat{M}_{k}\bigr)\circ\bigl(D^{\bot}\circ\hat{M}_{\mathit{ex}}\bigr),

which is the desired factorization. ∎

0.A.9 Proof of Theorem 5.1

Fix a well-typed global workflow PP over lifelines ℒ\mathscr{L}. We prove the two items.

(1) Completeness of realization. We show: for every M∈⟦P⟧M\in\llbracket P\rrbracket there exists M^∈⟦𝒟P⟧\hat{M}\in\llbracket\mathcal{D}_{P}\rrbracket with 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾⁡(M^)=M\mathsf{erase}(\hat{M})=M. Proceed by structural induction on PP.

Base cases: ε\varepsilon, 𝚖𝚜𝚐\mathtt{msg}, 𝚊𝚌𝚝\mathtt{act}. If P=εP=\varepsilon, take M^=Mε\hat{M}=M_{\varepsilon}. If PP is 𝚖𝚜𝚐\mathtt{msg}/𝚊𝚌𝚝\mathtt{act}, then πX​(P)\pi_{X}(P) produces exactly the corresponding local letters on the endpoints/owner and ε\varepsilon elsewhere, so the unique global one-step MSC (for that statement) is realized directly. No control letters occur, and thus 𝖾𝗋𝖺𝗌𝖾\mathsf{erase} is the identity.

If-construct. Let P=𝚒𝚏​c​@​B​𝚝𝚑𝚎𝚗​Q⊤​𝚎𝚕𝚜𝚎​Q⊥P=\mathtt{if}\ c@B\ \mathtt{then}\ Q_{\top}\ \mathtt{else}\ Q_{\bot} and M∈⟦P⟧M\in\llbracket P\rrbracket. Then either M=M𝗂𝖿⊤​(c​@​B)B∘M⊤M=M_{\mathsf{if}_{\top}(c@B)}^{B}\circ M_{\top} with M⊤∈⟦Q⊤⟧M_{\top}\in\llbracket Q_{\top}\rrbracket or M=M𝗂𝖿⊥​(c​@​B)B∘M⊥M=M_{\mathsf{if}_{\bot}(c@B)}^{B}\circ M_{\bot} with M⊥∈⟦Q⊥⟧M_{\bot}\in\llbracket Q_{\bot}\rrbracket. Assume the ⊤\top-case; the other case is analogous.
